title: Individual productivity triples, but company delivery only shrinks from 20 days to 17
dek: AI armed everyone, but the organization didn't get faster — because the weakest link isn't people, it's process. The real dividing line is whether you can transform processes and the organization, not whether you hand out tokens to employees.
why: A frontline CEO talks about building his own CEO AI, canceling weekly meetings, and using token consumption to identify elite performers — the mechanisms and numbers are concrete, and the decision hub section in the second half is the most valuable.
who: CEOs, CTOs, and HR leaders driving AI adoption, especially managers trying to figure out why individual productivity improved but the organization didn't get faster.
skip: The first 4 minutes of education scenario setup can be fast-forwarded; go straight to the barrel short-board case at 16:07.

points.h: Individual productivity triples, delivery only speeds up by three days
points.body: NetEase did a survey last year: a software requirement, from the product manager receiving it and producing a design draft to the feature going live, averaged 20 working days. After AI coding crossed the inflection point, many engineers doubled or even tripled to quintupled their personal efficiency, some tenfold. But for features of similar scope, the entire process only shrank from 20 days to 17. The reason is that a team completing a complex task is like a barrel: of 20 staves, 10 are engineers, 3 are product, 3 are testing. The engineer and product manager staves rise rapidly, but some staves aren't people — they're processes — and they don't improve at all. So AI adoption must clear three hurdles: cognition, applying it to individuals' short-range tasks, and transforming processes and the organization. The third is the hardest.

points.h: Cancel weekly meetings: AI syncs information, humans only solve problems
points.body: Ruan Liang asked friends who run companies whether they still hold weekly meetings; 99% said yes. Weekly meetings usually serve three purposes: sync information, discover problems and opportunities, and make decisions. Previously they held 2.5-hour weekly meetings, but the time spent on this meeting could be ten times 2.5 hours — every department prepared materials layer by layer, and information sync itself wasn't done well, because no one listened attentively the whole time and might miss a sentence relevant to them. After the reform: the general manager and management agreed on what information was needed, everyone filled in a template and stored it in the knowledge base, and AI scanned and integrated it into a focused, interactive HTML report where people could leave comments and follow-up questions; an AI agent produced a preliminary list of problems and opportunities, which human brains confirmed and supplemented; solving problems and making decisions became dedicated meetings.

points.h: SaaS isn't dead, but ordinary SaaS will die
points.body: Ruan Liang doesn't think SaaS is dead: SaaS is essentially Service, and Service always exists, just in different forms — AI as a Service and Agent as a Service are themselves software. But ordinary SaaS may indeed die; truly good SaaS that has entered a company's critical processes will instead get better and better, because it becomes internal infrastructure. Previously humans used software, limited by time and energy; in the future, a large number of Agents will call databases, APIs, security APIs, review APIs, HR APIs, CRM APIs — call volumes far exceeding the number and actions of humans, which will increase dramatically, and the more it's called, the more entrenched it becomes. The premise is that this Service itself is critical enough within the enterprise.

points.h: Distill top salespeople into skills and distribute to everyone
points.body: Bosses have two headaches: the sales team has only one or two strong performers and the rest are mediocre; or a salesperson is too strong — what if they leave? Previously there was no solution, but now you can distill or extract the actions, scripts, and behaviors of good salespeople into skills. Two uses: distribute them to other salespeople for direct use; and let AI turn elite salespeople into teachers to train ordinary salespeople. What training should distill isn't the salesperson, it's the customer — take the customer interaction data (calls, WeChat, emails, etc.) that salespeople have had contact with, and let AI simulate various customers to train salespeople. Online sales are purely digital and on record; for offline sales, it's recommended or even required to equip them with a recording card, and after a visit, while memory is fresh, record a two-to-three-minute voice memo, because salespeople dislike CRM (they think CRM is for managing them), but they don't mind a recording card, because it's also useful for their own customer review.

points.h: Fewer middle managers, strong individuals lead Agent legions back to the front line
points.body: Ruan Liang judges that middle managers will become fewer and fewer, but not necessarily eliminated — rather, they'll go to the front line, and the front line can also lead a bunch of agents. Middle managers with management responsibilities will become fewer and fewer, while elite individuals with strong skills will become more and more. He gives the example of an engineering team: previously, socialized division of labor made software development more and more specialized — front-end, back-end, algorithm, test engineers; in the past half year, it has clearly reverted to full-stack, everyone becoming full-end engineers. In the future, organizations will increasingly resemble a distributed structure, with countless highly capable engineers, one mother peak commanding some engineers, and countless agents fighting a battle. He envisions a future interview negotiation scenario: a candidate says, "I'm not one person, I bring an AI team, a summary of all my past experience and skills," and the premium the company pays might be some kind of OPC.

points.h: AI value formula: quality times time saved
points.body: Ruan Liang gives a formula referencing a paper: AI value = quality of AI completing the task (as a ratio of human quality) × time saved × the company's economic value per unit time. For example, a human makes a cup of coffee at 8 points, AI also makes it at 8 points, so the quality coefficient is 1; a human takes 20 minutes, AI takes only 10 seconds, saving 14 minutes 50 seconds; multiply by the company's economic value per unit time, and you can calculate ROI. Prioritize four types of tasks for AI: time-consuming, high-frequency, unavoidable, and tasks where different people produce roughly the same result. Once calculated, you can immediately decide whether to use AI. He also suggests first using the most expensive AI (Claude, GPT) to prove the task can be done, solidify the process, then switch to cheaper ones — if the most expensive can do it, within two months the cheaper ones can too.

points.h: Token consumption leads by a landslide, output also leads by a landslide
points.body: NetEase started a points system in 2024, trying to quantify engineers' work tasks into points with work value. By the AI era, they found a group of people whose token consumption was astonishing, and whose work output and work value were also astonishing, forming a statistical pattern: people whose token consumption leads by a landslide are most likely building systems for themselves, saving their own work time and increasing thinking time, so their work quality and results also lead by a landslide. Many bosses worry about AI abuse causing waste; Ruan Liang's hot take is that truly excellent or elite people won't waste — the company has audits but doesn't tell colleagues, and through statistics they found elite colleagues didn't waste. He also says small companies are more likely to fully embrace AI, because there are fewer organizational relationships, the boss uses it first, there are fewer layers, and the chain is shorter.

points.h: The core of a decision hub is decision history, not the model
points.body: Building an AI decision hub essentially requires a high-quality knowledge base, and what really matters is the historical decision-making process and decision basis. This year NetEase preserved historical decisions, incorporated them into the knowledge base, combined the two types of knowledge to train an agent or skill, then fed back hundreds of original cases for the agent to judge, achieving over 90% accuracy. Ruan Liang also mentions that Bridgewater Associates equipped researchers and analysts with agents they built themselves, precipitating the decision-making process and decision history into a decision knowledge base; what Bridgewater did better was making the agent a learnable, evolvable part — after a person adjusts it, the confirmed adjustment actions enter the next round of reinforcement, keeping pace with the times, equivalent to human-machine collaborative self-evolution.
